value.overview: The Buff-breasted Sandpiper is a medium-sized shorebird that breeds in the High Arctic of Alaska and Canada and migrates through the Americas to grasslands of Brazil, Uruguay, and Argentina. Unlike many sandpipers, it commonly feeds in dry, open habitats rather than muddy shorelines. Its long-distance journey depends on a connected network of tundra, grasslands, agricultural fields, and other suitable stopover sites.
value.classification: The Buff-breasted Sandpiper belongs to the sandpiper family Scolopacidae and the genus Calidris. Its scientific name is Calidris subruficollis.
value.identification: This elegant sandpiper has a warm buff-colored face, neck, breast, and upper belly, contrasting with a whiter lower belly. The back is brown with darker markings, and the head appears relatively large with a prominent dark eye. It has a short, straight, dark bill and medium-length yellowish legs. Juveniles usually show a crisp, scaly pattern on the back. Compared with Baird’s Sandpiper, it is more evenly buff-colored and has yellower legs.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds on dry, elevated tundra slopes, ridges, and river or stream margins in northern Alaska and Canada. During migration it uses open, sparsely vegetated areas such as short grasslands, wet pastures, plowed fields, rice fields, sod farms, and higher sections of beaches. It winters mainly in grasslands and agricultural landscapes of southern South America. In Costa Rica, it is a rare and irregular migrant, especially during southbound migration from late August through October. Records are associated with open grassy or agricultural wetlands, including sites such as Chomes and the Tempisque basin.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Costa Rica is primarily a rare autumn stopover country; spring passage may occur in March and April but is much less documented. Birds continue south to wintering grounds in South America.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in the High Arctic, where males gather at dispersed leks and perform energetic displays to attract females. The female selects a dry, well-drained site, usually near a stream or river, and makes a shallow ground scrape lined with nearby moss, lichens, leaves, or sedges. Clutches usually contain four eggs, with a reported range of two to five. The female alone incubates the eggs for about 23–25 days. Downy chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and feed themselves.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects, including beetles, ants, flies, midges, crane flies, moths, grasshoppers, and crickets. Spiders and small crustaceans are also taken during migration, and small amounts of seeds may be eaten. This sandpiper often feeds by sight, standing quietly before making a short run to seize prey from the ground surface. It generally does not probe deeply into soil or mud.
value.behavior: Buff-breasted Sandpipers are mostly terrestrial and often walk or run through short vegetation rather than wade in water. They may remain unusually still when alarmed. After breeding, they gather in migrating flocks, although individuals may also travel alone. Males establish display areas at leks during the breeding season, and some display behavior can occur during migration or on wintering grounds. On wintering areas, birds may become more dispersed and defend feeding territories.

conservation.populationTrend: Declining. Available assessments indicate a major long-term reduction, with additional declines in recent decades.
conservation.threats: Major threats include conversion and degradation of Arctic breeding habitat, loss of grasslands and other open habitats along migration routes and in South America, drainage of wetlands and agricultural stopover areas, and disturbance at important feeding sites. Historical overhunting caused severe declines, and climate change may further affect tundra conditions, weather during migration, and the availability of suitable grassland habitat.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore native grasslands, seasonal wetlands, rice landscapes, and other open stopover habitats. Support conservation of Arctic tundra and South American grasslands, and encourage bird-friendly agricultural practices that retain shallow wetlands and short vegetation. In Costa Rica, protect important sites such as Chomes and the Tempisque basin, avoid disturbing feeding flocks, and submit well-documented sightings to established bird-monitoring programs.
